summary: Budget day: Champagne tables Budget 2026 this afternoon with deep deficits expected, Ottawa says the US vote won't change its trade plan, and Ontario students walk out.
body: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tables the federal budget this afternoon. He says it will give Canada a "strong footing" in a volatile world, and that running deficits to help workers hurt by US tariffs is "the right thing to do"[^1]. Analysts expect deep deficits, slightly smaller than the $65.3 billion forecast in the spring; the Parliamentary Budget Officer, Parliament's independent fiscal watchdog, projects $63.3 billion this year[^2][^3]. The Liberals hold a majority, so the budget is expected to pass[^3].

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wants Prime Minister Mark Carney to cut spending and keep his promised "debt anchors", and is asking for a pause on federal diesel taxes and the GST on fuel[^4]. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says Tuesday's US midterm results "won't divert" Canada's plan to find new trade partners, and that talks with Washington are productive[^5].

For students: the Canadian Federation of Students–Ontario, an advocacy group, has called walkouts on more than 15 campuses today against a 2% tuition increase and OSAP changes that make at least 75% of student aid loans rather than grants[^7]. And Premier Doug Ford said there is "no 2.0" New Deal for Toronto, telling the city it must handle its own budget[^6].
differences: The Liberals say they are a year ahead on their goal of balancing day-to-day spending by 2027-28. The budget officer doubts it, and economists at Desjardins and the C.D. Howe Institute warn deficits could get worse once high oil prices fade[^2][^4].
